# Quantum groups and quantum affine algebras {#sec-quantum-groups}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Work with $U_q(sl_2)$ and its representations for generic $q$, for $\lvert q\rvert=1$ and at roots of unity.
- Use the Hopf-algebra structure: coproduct, antipode and counit.
- Define the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebras $U_q(\hat g)$ and their evaluation representations.
- Derive the Yang–Baxter equation, unitarity and crossing of R-matrices from the universal R-matrix.
- See the trigonometric six-vertex R-matrix appear as the R-matrix part of the sine-Gordon S-matrix.
:::

A symmetry of a quantum field theory acts on multi-particle states through a rule for combining the charges of the constituents. For an ordinary Lie group the rule is additive: a generator $X$ acts on a two-particle state as $X\otimes1+1\otimes X$. The non-local charges of sine-Gordon and of the imaginary-coupling affine Toda theories are not additive. They are built from line integrals of vertex operators, and the charge of a two-soliton state depends on the order of the solitons. Algebraically this means that the rule for combining charges, the **coproduct**, is not symmetric. The resulting structures are **quantum groups**. This chapter introduces them through $U_q(sl_2)$ and its affine extension, which is all that is needed to understand sine-Gordon, and then states the general definitions.

Throughout, $q\in\mathbb C^*$ is not a root of unity unless stated otherwise, and

$$
[n]_q=\frac{q^n-q^{-n}}{q-q^{-1}},\qquad[n]_q!=[1]_q[2]_q\cdots[n]_q .
$$

As $q\to1$, $[n]_q\to n$.

## $U_q(sl_2)$ {#sec-uqsl2}

The algebra $U_q(sl_2)$ is generated by $E$, $F$ and $K^{\pm1}$ with relations

$$
KEK^{-1}=q^2E,\qquad KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F,\qquad[E,F]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}} .
$$ {#eq-uqsl2}

Writing $K=q^H$ and letting $q\to1$ recovers $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, $[E,F]=H$, the Chevalley basis of $sl_2$.

**Representations.** For generic $q$ the finite-dimensional irreducible representations are deformations of those of $sl_2$. The spin-$j$ representation has a basis $v_0,\dots,v_{2j}$ with

$$
Kv_k=q^{2j-2k}v_k,\qquad Fv_k=v_{k+1},\qquad Ev_k=[k]_q[2j+1-k]_q\,v_{k-1},
$$ {#eq-spin-j}

with $v_{-1}=v_{2j+1}=0$. (There are also versions with $K$ replaced by $-K$, which we ignore.) For spin $\frac12$,

$$
E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad K=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\0&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-spin-half}

## Hopf algebras {#sec-hopf}

To act on tensor products, $U_q(sl_2)$ needs a coproduct $\Delta:U\to U\otimes U$, an algebra homomorphism that tells each generator how to act on two-particle states. We use

$$
\Delta(K)=K\otimes K,\qquad\Delta(E)=E\otimes K+1\otimes E,\qquad\Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes F .
$$ {#eq-coproduct}

It is coassociative, $(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta$, so it extends consistently to $N$-particle states. Together with the **counit** $\epsilon(E)=\epsilon(F)=0$, $\epsilon(K)=1$, which defines the trivial (vacuum) representation, and the **antipode**

$$
S(K)=K^{-1},\qquad S(E)=-EK^{-1},\qquad S(F)=-KF ,
$$ {#eq-antipode}

which defines the dual (antiparticle) representation, this makes $U_q(sl_2)$ a **Hopf algebra** [@kassel1995; @chari1994]. The antipode is an algebra anti-homomorphism, and the dual of a representation $\pi$ on $V$ is the representation $\pi^*(a)=\pi(S(a))^{\mathsf T}$ on $V^*$.

The coproduct is not **cocommutative**: $\Delta^{\rm op}=P\circ\Delta$, with $P$ the flip of tensor factors, differs from $\Delta$. As a consequence $V\otimes W$ and $W\otimes V$ are not related by the flip. They are, however, isomorphic, and the isomorphism is the R-matrix.

Also unlike the classical case, $S^2\ne1$. One checks that $S^2(a)=KaK^{-1}$. The double dual $V^{**}$ is therefore isomorphic to $V$ not by the canonical map but through $K$. In the affine case this "twist" becomes a shift of the spectral parameter, which is the algebraic origin of crossing (@sec-qg-crossing).

## The universal R-matrix {#sec-universal-r}

Drinfeld [@drinfeld1987] showed that $U_q(sl_2)$, suitably completed, contains an invertible element $\mathcal R\in U\otimes U$ with

$$
\mathcal R\,\Delta(a)\,\mathcal R^{-1}=\Delta^{\rm op}(a)\quad\text{for all }a ,
$$ {#eq-universal-r-intertwines}

$$
(\Delta\otimes1)\mathcal R=\mathcal R_{13}\mathcal R_{23},\qquad(1\otimes\Delta)\mathcal R=\mathcal R_{13}\mathcal R_{12} .
$$ {#eq-quasitriangular}

Explicitly, for the coproduct (-@eq-coproduct),

$$
\mathcal R=q^{\frac12H\otimes H}\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{q^{n(n-1)/2}(q-q^{-1})^n}{[n]_q!}\,E^n\otimes F^n .
$$ {#eq-universal-r-sl2}

A Hopf algebra with such an element is **quasitriangular**. Three consequences follow from (-@eq-universal-r-intertwines) and (-@eq-quasitriangular) by short manipulations [@chari1994]:

- the **Yang–Baxter equation** $\mathcal R_{12}\mathcal R_{13}\mathcal R_{23}=\mathcal R_{23}\mathcal R_{13}\mathcal R_{12}$;
- $(S\otimes1)\mathcal R=\mathcal R^{-1}$ and $(S\otimes S)\mathcal R=\mathcal R$;
- for representations $V$, $W$, the map $\check R_{VW}=P\circ(\pi_V\otimes\pi_W)(\mathcal R)$ intertwines $V\otimes W$ and $W\otimes V$.

On the spin-$\frac12$ representation only the terms $n=0,1$ survive, and in the basis $v_0\otimes v_0,v_0\otimes v_1,v_1\otimes v_0,v_1\otimes v_1$,

$$
(\pi_{\frac12}\otimes\pi_{\frac12})(\mathcal R)=q^{1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&q^{-1}&1-q^{-2}&0\\0&0&q^{-1}&0\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This R-matrix does not depend on a spectral parameter. To get the R-matrices of scattering theory, which do, we need the affine algebra.

## The quantum affine algebras $U_q(\hat g)$ {#sec-uqghat}

Let $\hat g$ be an affine algebra with Cartan matrix $a_{ij}$, $i,j=0,\dots,r$ (@sec-affine-algebras), and write $q_i=q^{\vec\alpha_i^2/2}$. The **Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum affine algebra** $U_q(\hat g)$ [@drinfeld1987; @jimbo1985] is generated by $e_i$, $f_i$, $k_i^{\pm1}$ with

$$
k_ik_j=k_jk_i,\qquad k_ie_jk_i^{-1}=q_i^{a_{ij}}e_j,\qquad k_if_jk_i^{-1}=q_i^{-a_{ij}}f_j,\qquad[e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}\frac{k_i-k_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},
$$

and the **$q$-Serre relations**, for $i\ne j$,

$$
\sum_{s=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^s\begin{bmatrix}1-a_{ij}\\ s\end{bmatrix}_{q_i}e_i^{1-a_{ij}-s}e_je_i^s=0 ,
$$

and the same with $f$ in place of $e$. Here $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}n\\s\end{smallmatrix}\right]_q=[n]_q!/([s]_q![n-s]_q!)$. These deform the Chevalley–Serre relations (-@eq-chevalley-serre). The coproduct, counit and antipode are given on each triple $(e_i,f_i,k_i)$ by (-@eq-coproduct)–(-@eq-antipode). The element $\prod_ik_i^{n_i}$, with the Kac labels $n_i$ of (-@eq-kac-labels), is central: conjugation by it multiplies $e_j$ by $q^{(\sum_in_i\vec\alpha_i)\cdot\vec\alpha_j}=1$. Since $k_i=q_i^{h_i}$ and $n_i^\vee=n_i\vec\alpha_i^2/2$, it equals $q^{\sum_in_i^\vee h_i}$, $q$ to the power of the central element. On the finite-dimensional representations used in this book it equals 1 (level zero).

The algebra $U_q(\hat g)$ is quasitriangular too, after adjoining the derivation $d$ and completing. Its universal R-matrix is an infinite product over the affine roots and is rarely written explicitly; what we use are its consequences.

**Evaluation representations and the spectral parameter.** A gradation $s$ of $\hat g$ (@sec-gradations) defines an automorphism of $U_q(\hat g)$, $e_i\mapsto x^{s_i}e_i$, $f_i\mapsto x^{-s_i}f_i$. Composing a representation $V$ with it gives the representation $V(x)$. For $U_q(\widehat{sl}_2)$ in the homogeneous gradation, the spin-$j$ representation of $U_q(sl_2)$ extends to a representation of $U_q(\widehat{sl}_2)$ by

$$
e_1=E,\quad f_1=F,\quad k_1=K,\qquad e_0=x\,F,\quad f_0=x^{-1}E,\quad k_0=K^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-evaluation-rep}

This is an **evaluation representation**. For other algebras, not every representation of $U_q(g)$ extends, and the smallest representations of $U_q(\hat g)$ that contain a given one (its **minimal affinizations**; for a multiple of a fundamental weight, the **Kirillov–Reshetikhin modules**) can be larger than the representation of $U_q(g)$ one starts from. Part VI meets examples: the $\mathbf{27}=\mathbf{26}\oplus\mathbf1$ of $U_q(e_6^{(2)})$ in @sec-sm-f4.

## R-matrices with spectral parameter {#sec-trigonometric-r}

Let $V(x)$ and $W(y)$ be finite-dimensional representations such that $V(x)\otimes W(y)$ is irreducible for generic $x/y$. Then, by Schur's lemma, there is a unique (up to normalization) intertwiner

$$
\check R_{VW}(x/y):V(x)\otimes W(y)\to W(y)\otimes V(x),\qquad\check R\,\Delta(a)=\Delta(a)\,\check R ,
$$ {#eq-r-check}

and it depends only on $x/y$. It is a rational function of $x/y$ (trigonometric in the rapidity), and we normalize it to equal 1 on the highest-weight vector. @sec-r-matrices explains how to compute it. Its three key properties follow from uniqueness and from the universal R-matrix.

**Yang–Baxter equation.** On $V_1(x_1)\otimes V_2(x_2)\otimes V_3(x_3)$, both sides of

$$
\check R_{12}\Big(\frac{x_2}{x_3}\Big)\check R_{23}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_3}\Big)\check R_{12}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\Big)
=\check R_{23}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\Big)\check R_{12}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_3}\Big)\check R_{23}\Big(\frac{x_2}{x_3}\Big)
$$ {#eq-ybe-braid}

intertwine $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3$ with $V_3\otimes V_2\otimes V_1$, and for generic parameters this intertwiner is unique. With the normalization fixed on highest-weight vectors, they are equal. In terms of $R=P\check R$ this is the Yang–Baxter equation (-@eq-yang-baxter) of scattering theory.

**Unitarity.** $\check R_{WV}(y/x)\check R_{VW}(x/y)$ intertwines $V(x)\otimes W(y)$ with itself, so it is a multiple of the identity, and the normalization makes it 1:

$$
\check R_{WV}(1/z)\,\check R_{VW}(z)=1 .
$$ {#eq-r-unitarity}

This is braiding unitarity (-@eq-braiding-unitarity). It contains no information about any inner product.

### Example: the six-vertex R-matrix {#sec-six-vertex}

For two spin-$\frac12$ evaluation representations (-@eq-evaluation-rep), solving (-@eq-r-check) (see @sec-jimbo-equations) gives, with $z=x/y$ and the basis order $v_0v_0,v_0v_1,v_1v_0,v_1v_1$,

$$
\check R(z)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&\dfrac{z(q^2-1)}{q^2-z}&\dfrac{q(z-1)}{z-q^2}&0\\[8pt]0&\dfrac{q(z-1)}{z-q^2}&\dfrac{q^2-1}{q^2-z}&0\\[2pt]0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-six-vertex}

One checks directly that it satisfies (-@eq-ybe-braid) and (-@eq-r-unitarity). Its eigenvalue on the $q$-symmetric (spin-1) part of $V\otimes V$ is 1, and on the $q$-antisymmetric (spin-0) part

$$
\rho_0(z)=\frac{1-q^2z}{z-q^2}.
$$ {#eq-six-vertex-eigenvalue}

**Sine-Gordon.** The S-matrix in the form $S(\theta)=S_0(\theta)\,P\check R(z)$ has diagonal entries $1$ and $b(z)=q(z-1)/(z-q^2)$ and off-diagonal entries proportional to $q^2-1$. Set

$$
z=e^{2\lambda\theta},\qquad q=-e^{i\pi\lambda},\qquad\lambda=\frac{8\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}^2}-1 .
$$

Then $b=\sinh\lambda\theta/\sinh\lambda(i\pi-\theta)$, which is $S_T/S_0$ of (-@eq-sg-smatrix), and the off-diagonal entries are $e^{\mp\lambda\theta}\sinh(i\pi\lambda)/\sinh\lambda(i\pi-\theta)$. The factors $e^{\mp\lambda\theta}$ are removed by a rapidity-dependent change of basis, which is the passage from the homogeneous to the principal gradation, and the result is $S_R/S_0$. So the sine-Gordon S-matrix is the six-vertex R-matrix times the scalar $S_0$, with $q=-e^{i\pi\lambda}=e^{8\pi^2i/\beta_{\rm SG}^2}$, in agreement with @sec-sg-quantum-group.

Part VI uses the opposite coproduct, $\Delta(e_i)=e_i\otimes1+k_i\otimes e_i$, $\Delta(f_i)=f_i\otimes k_i^{-1}+1\otimes f_i$, the form in which the non-local charges act (@sec-qg-coproduct). Since $P\check R(1/z)P$ intertwines the opposite coproduct, its six-vertex matrix is (-@eq-six-vertex) with $q\to q^{-1}$, at the same $z$, gradation and normalization, and the sine-Gordon value becomes $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}=e^{-8\pi^2i/\beta_{\rm SG}^2}$, that of Bernard and LeClair [@bernard1991]. The sign of $q$ cannot be absorbed in a change of basis. The substitution $q\to-q$ leaves the off-diagonal entries $c,c'$ of $P\check R$ and the crossing point $x_c=q^2$ of @sec-qg-crossing unchanged, but it reverses $b$. With it, it reverses the basis-independent combination $(1+b^2-cc')/2b=(q+q^{-1})/2$ and the factor $c_u$ of @sec-qg-crossing. It is conjugation of $\check R$ by $\mathrm{diag}(1,1,-1,1)$, which is not of the form $A\otimes A$. It changes the relative exchange sign of soliton and antisoliton, and it is what the crossing test of @sec-crossing-sign detects.

## Crossing from the antipode {#sec-qg-crossing}

The dual representation $V^*$ of an evaluation representation is again an evaluation representation, with a shifted spectral parameter: $V(x)^*\cong\bar V(x\,x_c)$ for some **crossing point** $x_c$, via a charge-conjugation matrix $C$, with $\bar V$ the conjugate (antiparticle) representation ($\bar V=V$ for $U_q(\widehat{sl}_2)$). For self-conjugate $V$, applying $\pi_V^*\otimes\pi_W$ to $(S\otimes1)\mathcal R=\mathcal R^{-1}$ gives

$$
\big(R(z)^{-1}\big)^{t_1}=c_u(z)\,(C^{-1}\otimes1)\,R(z\,x_c)\,(C\otimes1),
$$ {#eq-r-crossing}

with $R=P\check R$, $t_1$ the transpose in the first factor, and a scalar function $c_u(z)$ that the normalization introduces. This is the form used in @sec-unitarity-crossing. For the S-matrix $S(\theta)=\Phi(\theta)R(z(\theta))$ to be crossing symmetric, the crossing transformation $\theta\to i\pi-\theta$ must map $z$ to $x_c/z$, which ties the rapidity dependence of $z$ to $q$, and the scalar factor must absorb $c_u$.

**Example.** For the six-vertex R-matrix (-@eq-six-vertex), a direct computation gives $x_c=q^2$, $C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-q&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $c_u(z)=q(z-1)/(q^2z-1)$. With $z=e^{2\lambda\theta}$, crossing requires $e^{2\pi i\lambda}=q^2$, which is the relation found above.

The crossing point is a shadow of $S^2\ne1$. In $U_q(\hat g)$, $S^2(e_i)=q_i^2e_i$ and $S^2(f_i)=q_i^{-2}f_i$, so $S^2$ is conjugation by $q^{2\hat\rho}$, $\hat\rho=\bar\rho+h^\vee\Lambda_0$. Its $\Lambda_0$ part multiplies $e_0$ by $q^{2h^\vee}$, which in the homogeneous gradation is a rescaling of $x$, so $V(x)^{**}\cong V(x\,q^{2h^\vee})$ [@frenkel1992; @chari1994]. Here $q_i=q^{(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)/2}$ with $(\alpha_0,\alpha_0)=2$. For untwisted algebras this is the normalization of @sec-lie-algebraic-data; for twisted ones the short roots then have squared length 2. And $h^\vee$ is the dual Coxeter number of the algebra whose quantum group acts, which for the solitons of the Toda theory of $\hat g$ is $\hat g^\vee$. With the opposite coproduct of Part VI the shift is $q^{-2h^\vee}$. If $V(x)^*\cong V(x\,x_c)$, crossing twice gives $x_c^2=q^{2h^\vee}$, which fixes $x_c$ only up to a sign; for $U_q(\widehat{sl}_2)$, $x_c=q^2$ and $x_c^2=q^4=q^{2h^\vee}$. In the gradation of @sec-amplitude-and-gradation the crossing point is $x(i\pi)=e^{2\pi iT}$. The power of $q$ in it is the $S^2$ shift, and the dual Coxeter number of the Toda algebra in $T$ supplies only the sign that $S^2$ leaves open. In practice, Part VI computes $x_c$ numerically for each representation.

## Hermitian forms for $\lvert q\rvert=1$ {#sec-qg-hermitian}

In the imaginary-coupling theories $q$ is a phase. For $\lvert q\rvert=1$, the assignment

$$
E^*=F,\qquad F^*=E,\qquad K^*=K^{-1}
$$

extended antilinearly and anti-multiplicatively is consistent with (-@eq-uqsl2), because $\bar q=q^{-1}$. On the spin-$\frac12$ representation (-@eq-spin-half) it is the ordinary Hermitian conjugate, so this representation is unitary. But two features differ from the classical case.

- **Indefinite forms.** On the spin-1 representation, the invariant form has $\langle Fv_0,Fv_0\rangle=\langle v_0,EFv_0\rangle=[2]_q\langle v_0,v_0\rangle$, and $[2]_q=q+q^{-1}=2\cos\gamma$ for $q=e^{i\gamma}$. For $\pi/2<\gamma<\pi$ this is negative: the invariant Hermitian form is indefinite. Higher representations have forms whose signature is governed by the signs of $q$-numbers.
- **Reversal of tensor factors.** The $*$-operation is not compatible with $\Delta$, but with $\Delta^{\rm op}$: $(*\otimes*)\circ\Delta=\Delta^{\rm op}\circ*$. An invariant Hermitian form on $V\otimes W$ therefore pairs $V\otimes W$ with $W\otimes V$, and to turn it into a form on a single space one needs an intertwiner, that is, an R-matrix.

The second point is why the S-matrices of the imaginary-coupling theories are generally not Hermitian analytic in the soliton basis, and why the question of unitarity depends on the choice of basis [@miramontes1999]. Part VII returns to it (@sec-scattering).

## Roots of unity {#sec-roots-of-unity}

If $q^{2p}=1$ for some integer $p$, then $[p]_q=0$ and the representation theory changes. In (-@eq-spin-j) with $2j+1>p$, the vector $v_p$ satisfies $Ev_p=[p]_q[2j+1-p]_qv_{p-1}=0$, so it generates a proper subrepresentation, and the spin-$j$ representation is no longer irreducible. The well-behaved representations are those with $2j+1<p$, and in tensor products of these, the summands with highest weight $j\ge(p-1)/2$ (irreducible for $2j+1=p$, where $[p]_q=0$, indecomposable but reducible for $2j+1>p$) have **quantum dimension** zero. They can be consistently discarded, leaving a truncated tensor product with finitely many representations. This truncation is the algebraic basis of **RSOS restriction**: in the S-matrix it keeps only kink states whose vacua are labelled by the allowed spins (@sec-sg-quantum-group, @sec-rsos).

## Exercises {#sec-quantum-groups-exercises}

::: {#exr-coproduct-homomorphism}
Check that $\Delta$ of (-@eq-coproduct) respects the relations (-@eq-uqsl2): in particular $[\Delta(E),\Delta(F)]=(\Delta(K)-\Delta(K)^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$.
:::

::: {#exr-antipode}
Verify the antipode axiom $m\circ(S\otimes1)\circ\Delta=\eta\circ\epsilon$ on $E$, $F$ and $K$, and show $S^2(a)=KaK^{-1}$.
:::

::: {#exr-spin-j}
Check that (-@eq-spin-j) defines a representation, and that it reduces to the usual spin-$j$ representation of $sl_2$ as $q\to1$ (after rescaling the basis).
:::

::: {#exr-six-vertex}
Show that (-@eq-six-vertex) satisfies $\check R(z)\check R(1/z)=1$, and that its eigenvalues are $1$ (three times) and $\rho_0(z)$. At which value of $z$ is $\check R$ proportional to the projector onto the spin-1 part, and at which does it have a pole whose residue is proportional to the projector onto spin 0?
:::

::: {#exr-sg-match}
Carry out the substitution $z=e^{2\lambda\theta}$, $q=-e^{i\pi\lambda}$ in (-@eq-six-vertex), and find the diagonal change of basis on each one-soliton space that turns the off-diagonal entries of $P\check R$ into $S_R/S_0$.
:::

::: {#exr-hermitian-spin1}
For $q=e^{i\gamma}$, find the invariant Hermitian form on the spin-1 representation and its signature as a function of $\gamma$. For which $\gamma$ is the spin-1 representation unitary?
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-quantum-groups-notes}

Quantum groups were introduced by Drinfeld [@drinfeld1987] and Jimbo [@jimbo1985]; Jimbo [-@jimbo1986] computed the R-matrices in the vector representations of all the classical quantum affine algebras, with the affine Toda equations in mind. Kassel [@kassel1995] is a gentle introduction to Hopf algebras and $U_q(sl_2)$, Chari and Pressley [@chari1994] the standard reference for quantum affine algebras, and Gómez, Ruiz-Altaba and Sierra [@gomez1996] a physics-oriented treatment including RSOS models. That the axioms of the S-matrix bootstrap (crossing, bootstrap, braiding unitarity) follow from the Hopf-algebra structure, and that the gradation is fixed by Lorentz spin, is shown in [@delius1995].
